paragraphs: Soils hold more carbon than the atmosphere and all living vegetation combined, so small changes in how much they store can matter for the climate. For years the prevailing view was that carbon persists in soil mainly because its chemistry makes it resistant to decay: complex molecules, it was thought, simply last longer. Newer work stresses a different explanation. Even simple molecules can remain for centuries if they cling to mineral grains or sit in pockets too small for microbes to enter. If that is correct, the amount of carbon a soil stores depends less on the plant material added to it than on the structure and mineral content of the soil itself, a conclusion with practical consequences for efforts to increase storage by changing farm practices.
